idiom_name: legacy facade implementing the frozen interface + System.Text.Json converters
implementation_notes: A class implements the frozen legacy interface - usually explicitly, so the old members do not appear on the new API surface - and delegates to the modernized service, while System.Text.Json pins the old wire shape: [JsonPropertyName] carries the frozen field names and a custom JsonConverter<T> with Read/Write overrides handles everything that is not a straight property copy (text decimals, legacy date formats, defaults for absent fields). The custom converter is the documented escape hatch for exactly this situation, since the built-in converters cover the current .NET conventions rather than an older contract. The classic hand-written facade is still justified when the legacy surface is COM/interop or a binary boundary; for a shape that differs only in names and defaults, converters plus a DTO are enough and no window class is needed at all.
pitfalls: Converter behaviour is a composition of defaults (naming policy, number handling, null versus absent): pin every one of them per property, or the old shape shifts silently between runtimes.

A synchronous legacy interface that blocks on the new asynchronous core (.Result or .Wait()) can deadlock under a synchronization context; block only in a dedicated boundary path, never inside a UI or request context.
